Utility cost-of-service studies often allocate demand-related delivery costs across
customer classes using each class's **non-coincident peak (NCP)** — the maximum demand that
class ever reaches, regardless of when it happens. That method implicitly assumes every
class's peak matters equally, no matter its timing. But heat-pump homes tend to peak on cold
winter mornings, while today's dominant natural-gas-heated population still peaks on hot
summer afternoons (running air conditioning). An NCP allocator conflates *how big* a class's
peak is with *when* it happens — and can assign heat-pump customers a disproportionate share
of delivery costs relative to their actual share of the customer population.

This notebook reproduces that argument for MD BGE, computing each residential heating-type
subclass's (heat pump, natural gas, oil/propane, electric resistance) hourly load, its own
peak magnitude and timing, and its resulting share of a hypothetical NCP-based cost
allocation — purely from ResStock hourly load curves. It deliberately stops there: it does
**not** attempt a dollar-denominated, voltage-level embedded-cost allocation (the way RI's
`embedded_costs.qmd` does), because that requires BGE's own multi-voltage embedded cost of
service study (ECOSS) workpapers, which aren't yet available for this analysis (tracked
separately, not in scope for RDP-264). What follows is the one piece of that RI notebook that
actually made it into testimony — the NCP-share argument alone, generalized to run against
any state/utility/batch.

The functions doing the data crunching live in
[`lib/rates_analysis/ncp_funcs.py`](../../../lib/rates_analysis/ncp_funcs.py). This notebook
just calls those with MD BGE's specific state/batch/scenario values from `batch_config.yaml`.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup

from __future__ import annotations

import pickle
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
import yaml
from great_tables import GT

from lib.great_tables import get_switchbox_gt_tab_options
from lib.quarto import display_gt
from lib.rates_analysis.ncp_funcs import (
    aggregate_hourly_by_subclass,
    compute_subclass_ncp_shares,
    load_subclass_population,
    scan_hourly_loads_for_buildings,
    subclass_ncp_report_vars,
    validate_hourly_against_annual_kwh,
)
from lib.rates_analysis.rate_case_funcs import (
    HEATING_ORDER,
    HEATING_TYPE_LABELS,
    load_billing_kwh_annual,
    segment_name,
)

report_vars: dict = {}
```

## Parameters

Batch identity lives in `batch_config.yaml` alongside this report, not hardcoded here, so
re-running against a new batch is a one-file change. `RESSTOCK_RELEASE` and `UPGRADE` point at
the Switchbox-corrected (`_sb`) ResStock release CAIRO's inputs are drawn from — upgrade `00`
is today's mixed heating population (pre-retrofit), the same population `analysis.qmd` and
`incremental_cos.qmd` use for their pre-retrofit numbers. We prefer the local EBS mirror of
that release over S3 when it's present, since `scan_hourly_loads_for_buildings` opens one
parquet file per building — thousands of S3 GETs for a full state — and local disk skips that
per-file network overhead entirely.

```{python}
#| label: params

_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())

STATE = _batch_config["STATE"]
BATCH = _batch_config["BATCH"]
DEFAULT_SCENARIO = _batch_config["BASELINE_BILL_SCENARIO"]
RESSTOCK_RELEASE = _batch_config["RESSTOCK_RELEASE"]
UTILITY = "bge"
UPGRADE = "00"

_local_resstock = Path(f"/ebs/data/nrel/resstock/{RESSTOCK_RELEASE}")
PATH_RESSTOCK_RELEASE = (
    str(_local_resstock) if _local_resstock.exists() else f"s3://data.sb/nrel/resstock/{RESSTOCK_RELEASE}"
)

SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC = segment_name(DEFAULT_SCENARIO, "precalc")

print(f"state={STATE}  utility={UTILITY}  batch={BATCH}  upgrade={UPGRADE}")
print(f"resstock_release={PATH_RESSTOCK_RELEASE}")
```

## Subclass population

We start from CAIRO's own master bills table, which already classifies every building into a
heating-type-v2 subclass (`heat_pump`, `natgas`, `delivered_fuels` — oil or propane —,
`electrical_resistance`, or `other`) and assigns it to a utility. Reusing CAIRO's
classification (rather than re-deriving it from raw ResStock metadata) keeps this consistent
with every other MD BGE notebook and avoids a separate `buildstock_fetch` dependency just to
identify heating type.

```{python}
#| label: load-population

population = load_subclass_population(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, UTILITY).collect()
population.head()
```

```{python}
#| label: population-counts

(
    population.group_by("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("n_buildings"), pl.col("weight").sum().alias("weighted_customers"))
    .sort("weighted_customers", descending=True)
)
```

MD BGE's residential population in this batch has `{python} f"{population.height:,}"` sampled
buildings, representing `{python} f"{population['weight'].sum():,.0f}"` weighted customers
across the five subclasses above.

```{python}
#| label: bldg-ids

bldg_ids = population["bldg_id"].to_list()
```

## Hourly loads

For every building in that population, we scan its raw ResStock hourly load curve directly
from S3 and compute **grid consumption** — `max(total_load - abs(pv), 0)` — the same formula
CAIRO itself bills against
([`rate-design-platform/utils/loads.py`](https://github.com/switchbox-data/rate-design-platform/blob/main/utils/loads.py)).
This matters: RI's original `embedded_costs.qmd` summed `out.electricity.net.energy_consumption`
instead, which that module documents as diverging from `total` by up to ~10% even for
non-solar buildings. We build each building's parquet path directly from its `bldg_id`
(rather than scanning the whole state's `load_curve_hourly` partition and filtering), since
MD BGE is a small fraction of that partition.

```{python}
#| label: scan-hourly

hourly = scan_hourly_loads_for_buildings(PATH_RESSTOCK_RELEASE, STATE, UPGRADE, bldg_ids)
hourly.head().collect()
```

## Validating against CAIRO's own billed kWh

Before trusting these hourly loads for anything, we check them against CAIRO's own
per-building annual kWh export (`billing_kwh_annual.parquet`, read via
`rate_case_funcs.load_billing_kwh_annual()`). CAIRO can apply a uniform
`resstock_kwh_scale_factor` to a utility's loads before billing (to match a rate case's
test-year kWh) — see
[`rate-design-platform/utils/pre/rev_requirement/README.md`](https://github.com/switchbox-data/rate-design-platform/blob/main/utils/pre/rev_requirement/README.md)
— so we don't expect our raw hourly sum to equal CAIRO's billed annual kWh 1:1 even when
methodology is fully aligned. `validate_hourly_against_annual_kwh()` handles this by
discovering that scale factor empirically (the *median* per-building ratio of CAIRO's value
to ours) rather than hardcoding it from a separate repo's per-batch config, and flags any
building whose own ratio departs meaningfully from that population-wide median — a real
per-building mismatch, not just the expected uniform scaling.

```{python}
#| label: validate-hourly-vs-annual

computed_annual = (
    hourly.group_by("bldg_id")
    .agg(pl.col("grid_kwh").sum().alias("computed_annual_kwh_grid"))
    .collect()
)
reference_annual = load_billing_kwh_annual(STATE, UTILITY, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC)

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught_warnings:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    kwh_comparison = validate_hourly_against_annual_kwh(computed_annual, reference_annual)
    for _w in caught_warnings:
        print(f"WARNING: {_w.message}")

kwh_comparison.describe()
```

The median ratio above (`annual_kwh_grid / computed_annual_kwh_grid`) is CAIRO's implied
`resstock_kwh_scale_factor` for MD BGE in this batch. A warning naming a count of buildings
outside tolerance is expected here — real ResStock buildings show some
`out.electricity.net`/`out.electricity.total` calibration drift beyond the shared scale
factor, which is exactly what this check surfaces. Crucially, **this doesn't undermine the
NCP-share analysis below**: a uniform scale factor multiplies every building's every hour by
the same constant, so it cancels out entirely in a *share* calculation (each subclass's peak
divided by the sum of all subclasses' peaks). The outlier buildings this check flags are a
data-quality note for future work, not a reason to distrust the shares that follow.

## Aggregating to subclass hourly loads

Next we weight each building's hourly grid consumption by its ResStock sample weight and sum
within each subclass, producing one weighted hourly load curve per heating-type subclass —
the shape each subclass's peak will be read off of.

```{python}
#| label: aggregate-by-subclass

aggregate_curves = aggregate_hourly_by_subclass(hourly, population)
aggregate_curves.head()
```

## Subclass NCP shares

For each subclass we now take its own maximum hourly weighted load (its "secondary NCP") and
the timestamp it occurs at, then divide by the sum of every subclass's own maximum to get that
subclass's share of a hypothetical NCP-based cost allocation. We use the full year (not a
summer-only window), matching what RI's testimony actually reported.

```{python}
#| label: compute-ncp-shares

ncp_shares = compute_subclass_ncp_shares(aggregate_curves, only_consider_summer_peaks=False)
ncp_shares
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-subclass-ncp-shares
#| tbl-cap: "Each residential heating-type subclass's share of customers versus its share of a hypothetical non-coincident-peak (NCP) cost allocation, and the timestamp of its own peak (MD BGE, ResStock upgrade 00)."

_ncp_display = (
    ncp_shares.with_columns(
        pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2")
        .replace_strict(HEATING_TYPE_LABELS, default=pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2"))
        .alias("heating_type")
    )
    .with_columns(pl.col("heating_type").cast(pl.Enum(HEATING_ORDER)))
    .sort("heating_type")
    .select(
        "heating_type",
        "num_homes_pct_of_total",
        "subclass_pct_of_class_share",
        "ncp_timestamp",
        "secondary_ncp_raw",
        "annual_kwh",
    )
)

_ncp_gt = (
    GT(_ncp_display, rowname_col="heating_type")
    .fmt_percent(columns=["num_homes_pct_of_total", "subclass_pct_of_class_share"], scale_values=False, decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns=["secondary_ncp_raw", "annual_kwh"], decimals=0)
    .cols_label(
        num_homes_pct_of_total="Share of customers",
        subclass_pct_of_class_share="Share of NCP allocation",
        ncp_timestamp="Own peak occurs at",
        secondary_ncp_raw="Own peak (weighted kW)",
        annual_kwh="Annual weighted kWh",
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label="Baseline heating type")
    .tab_source_note(
        "Share of NCP allocation = this subclass's own hourly peak ÷ the sum of every "
        "subclass's own hourly peak. Peaks are each subclass's own maximum weighted hourly "
        "grid consumption across the full year, not a single coincident system peak."
    )
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_ncp_gt)
```

```{python}
#| label: extract-report-vars

report_vars.update(subclass_ncp_report_vars(ncp_shares))
report_vars
```

Heat pump customers are `{python} f"{report_vars['hp_pct_of_customers']:.0f}%"` of MD BGE's
residential population, but would account for
`{python} f"{report_vars['hp_ncp_share_pct']:.0f}%"` of an NCP-based delivery cost allocation
— disproportionate to their customer share. Their own peak occurs at
`{python} report_vars['hp_ncp_timestamp'].strftime("%B %-d, %Y at %-I %p")`, a winter morning.
Natural-gas-heated customers, still the largest subclass at
`{python} f"{report_vars['natgas_pct_of_customers']:.0f}%"` of customers, would receive only
`{python} f"{report_vars['natgas_ncp_share_pct']:.0f}%"` of that same allocation, with their
own peak at `{python} report_vars['natgas_ncp_timestamp'].strftime("%B %-d, %Y at %-I %p")` —
a summer afternoon. An NCP allocator scores each subclass on its own peak in isolation, so it
never has to reconcile that these two subclasses aren't even peaking at the same time of year.

## Export report variables

This notebook writes to its own cache file (`ncp_report_variables.pkl`), separate from
`analysis.qmd`'s `report_variables.pkl`, since both are rendered in the same Quarto project
and a shared, fully-overwritten cache file would let whichever notebook renders last silently
clobber the other's variables.

```{python}
#| label: export-report-vars

Path("../cache").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("../cache/ncp_report_variables.pkl").write_bytes(pickle.dumps(report_vars))
```
